subject: Vocabulary
description: Latin roots LOQU/LOC (speak) and LECT/LEG (read, choose, gather) — eloquent, soliloquy, dialect, election, lecture, intellect.

questions.stem: The root LOQU/LOC means 'to speak'. A LOQUACIOUS person is:
questions.explanation: LOQUACIOUS — adjective meaning 'TALKATIVE, given to constant talking, chatty'. Root LOQU = speak. ETYMOLOGY: Latin 'loqui' = to speak. WORD FAMILY: (1) ELOQUENT (out + speak) — fluent and persuasive in speech. (2) SOLILOQUY (alone + speak) — a speech to oneself, famous in drama (Hamlet's 'To be or not to be' is the most famous English soliloquy). (3) COLLOQUIAL (together + speak) — informal, conversational language. (4) VENTRILOQUIST (belly + speak) — entertainer who throws their voice. (5) LOCUTION = a particular phrase or expression. (6) CIRCUMLOCUTION (around + speak) — using too many words to say something simple. (7) GRANDILOQUENT (grand + speak) — pompous, lofty in speech. SAMPLE SENTENCE: 'The loquacious salesman talked us through every product feature for an hour.' SYNONYMS: garrulous, voluble, verbose. ANTONYMS: taciturn, reticent, laconic. PYQ FREQUENCY: vocab roots are top SSC CGL, CAT, IBPS PO English MCQ; ~2 per paper.

questions.explanation: ELOQUENT — fluent, articulate, and persuasive in speech or writing; expressing oneself effectively. ETYMOLOGY: ex (out) + loqui (speak) → 'speaking out powerfully'. NOUN: ELOQUENCE — the quality of being eloquent. SAMPLE: 'Lincoln's Gettysburg Address remains a masterpiece of eloquent oratory'. SYNONYMS: articulate, fluent, persuasive, silver-tongued. ANTONYMS: inarticulate, halting, tongue-tied, fumbling. KEY DISTINCTION: 'eloquent' implies BOTH fluency AND power/persuasiveness; merely talking a lot (loquacious) isn't enough. EXAM-FAVOURITE TRAP: students confuse ELOQUENT (fluent in speech) with ELEGANT (graceful in style) — different roots: elegant is from 'eligere' = to choose. CONTEXT: in literature, an 'eloquent silence' is a non-verbal moment that conveys deep meaning — example of figurative usage. PYQ FREQUENCY: ELOQUENT appears in SSC CGL, CAT, IBPS PO synonym/antonym MCQs 1-2× per cycle.

questions.explanation: SOLILOQUY = a dramatic speech delivered by a character ALONE on stage, expressing inner thoughts to the audience (without other characters hearing). ETYMOLOGY: solus (alone) + loqui (speak) = 'speaking alone'. FAMOUS EXAMPLES: (1) HAMLET — 'To be, or not to be, that is the question...' (Shakespeare, ~1600). (2) MACBETH — 'Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow, creeps in this petty pace...' (3) KING LEAR — 'Blow, winds, and crack your cheeks!' DISTINCTION: (a) DIALOGUE = two or more characters speaking. (b) MONOLOGUE = long speech by ONE character to OTHERS on stage. (c) SOLILOQUY = character ALONE, thinking aloud — audience overhears the thoughts. (d) ASIDE = brief comment to the audience while other characters can't hear. ROOT: 'solus' also gives us SOLO (alone), SOLITUDE (state of being alone), SOLITARY, DESOLATE. SHAKESPEARE'S PLAYS contain ~30+ major soliloquies; they remain the gold standard. PYQ FREQUENCY: literary terms in CAT, UPSC, MA Eng entrance MCQs.

questions.stem: The root LECT/LEG means 'read, choose, gather'. INTELLECT literally means:
questions.explanation: INTELLECT — etymology 'inter' (between) + 'lect/leg' (choose, gather) = the FACULTY OF CHOOSING BETWEEN, hence the rational mind, the power of reasoning. WORD FAMILY (root LECT/LEG = read, choose, gather): (1) LECTURE — a reading; an educational talk. (2) LEGEND — what is to be read; a story. (3) LEGIBLE — readable, capable of being read. (4) LEGION — a gathering of soldiers (Roman military unit of ~5,000). (5) ELECT — to choose out, select. (6) ELECTION — the act of choosing (especially political). (7) SELECT — to choose carefully. (8) COLLECT — to gather together. (9) COLLEGE — a gathering of scholars. (10) NEGLECT (neg + lect) = NOT to gather/pick up. (11) ELIGIBLE — fit to be chosen. (12) ECLECTIC — choosing from various sources. EXAM-FAVOURITE: trace word back to root → lock in meaning instantly. SAMPLE SENTENCE: 'Her intellect impressed everyone in the debate.' PYQ FREQUENCY: root-based vocab is the TOP CAT/CGL English-section trick — 2-3 per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: rewards systematic root-knowledge over rote memorization.

questions.stem: ECLECTIC, from the LECT root, describes a person/style that:
questions.explanation: ECLECTIC — adjective: choosing from a wide variety of styles, ideas, sources, methods. ETYMOLOGY: Greek 'eklektikos' = ek (out) + legein (choose) — to pick out. SAMPLE USAGES: 'an eclectic music collection' (mix of jazz, classical, rock); 'eclectic taste in art' (open to many genres); 'eclectic philosophy' (drawn from multiple traditions). PHILOSOPHICAL: in philosophy, ECLECTICISM is the practice of drawing from many schools rather than dogmatically following one. SYNONYMS: diverse, varied, wide-ranging, catholic (lowercase, meaning broad-minded). NEAR-SYNONYMS: heterogeneous (mixed in nature), miscellaneous (assorted). ANTONYMS: dogmatic, monolithic, narrow, rigid. POSITIVE CONNOTATION: 'eclectic' is usually praiseful — implies sophistication and openness. EXAM TRAP: students confuse ECLECTIC with ELECTIC (no such word) or EXOTIC (foreign-sourced) or ESOTERIC (hidden, only-for-insiders). PYQ FREQUENCY: ECLECTIC appears in CAT, GRE, UPSC PT high-vocab MCQs 1× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests advanced English for elite admissions.

questions.stem: DIALECT, from the LECT root, refers to:
questions.explanation: DIALECT — etymology 'dia' (across, through) + 'lect' (speak, read) = a regional or social variety of a language with distinct vocabulary, grammar, pronunciation. EXAMPLES: (1) ENGLISH dialects: British English (Cockney, Geordie, Scouse), American English (Southern, New England, AAVE), Indian English (Hinglish, Banglish, etc.). (2) HINDI dialects: Awadhi, Bhojpuri, Maithili, Brij Bhasha, Khariboli, Haryanvi, Marwari. (3) CHINESE: Mandarin, Cantonese, Wu, Hakka — though some linguists treat them as separate languages. (4) ARABIC: Egyptian, Levantine, Gulf, Maghrebi — mutually intelligible to varying degrees. SAMPLE: 'In rural Bengal, the spoken dialect differs significantly from the literary Bengali of Kolkata.' DISTINCTION: (a) LANGUAGE = a system; (b) DIALECT = a regional variety; (c) ACCENT = pronunciation only; (d) IDIOLECT = an individual's unique speech. POLITICAL ANGLE: 'A language is a dialect with an army and navy' (Max Weinreich) — the line between dialect and language is often political, not linguistic. PYQ FREQUENCY: DIALECT in CAT, IBPS English — 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: The word COLLOQUIAL, from LOQU root, means:
questions.explanation: COLLOQUIAL — adjective describing INFORMAL, EVERYDAY conversational language, as opposed to formal/literary writing. ETYMOLOGY: 'col' (with, together) + 'loqui' (speak) = 'speaking together' (i.e., as in casual conversation). EXAMPLES of COLLOQUIAL English: 'gonna' (going to), 'wanna' (want to), 'kid' (child), 'guy' (person), 'cool' (good), 'ain't' (isn't/aren't). DISTINCTION: (a) FORMAL: 'I would like to inquire about your well-being.' (b) COLLOQUIAL: 'How're you doing?' (c) SLANG: 'How's it hanging?' (very informal, often regional). NOUN: COLLOQUIALISM — an instance of casual expression. EXAM USE: in error-spotting Qs, COLLOQUIAL phrases are often INCORRECT in formal English contexts (academic writing, official letters). KEY DISTINCTION from related words: COLLOQUIAL (everyday) vs COLLOQUY (formal conversation, dialogue) — the noun 'colloquy' is FORMAL, while the adjective 'colloquial' describes INFORMAL speech. PYQ FREQUENCY: COLLOQUIAL appears in SSC CGL, CAT vocabulary 1× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: rewards register-awareness in English usage.
